# Markdown

Markdown is a _simple_ "markup" language. 

> A markup language allows you to format a document with **commands** instead of 
menu items. 

For instance, you can :

- Enclose a word between two sets of \*\*two asteriks\*\* to obtain **bold text**.
- Enclose a word between \_underscores\_ to produce _italic text_.
- Create headers, subheaders at various levels with `#`, `##` and `###`.
- Define a quote block by placing `>` in front of the quote. 

Markdown can be rendered in various formats, e.g. `html`, `pdf` and MSWord. 

# R Markdown 

R Markdown combines **text written with Markdown** and **code written with R**. This is useful in two ways: 

- **As a tool for analysis**: R Markdown replaces scripts when carrying analyses. You can **execute the R Code** contained in the R Markdown document to analyse your data. Moreover, since it allows for text, it can be used to **document your data analysis**. 


- **As a reporting tool**: Can also produce reports in various formats, including `.pdf`, `.docx`, and `html`. The latter option allows more interactivity thanks to the `html` options.

## Create a new R markdown document

This can be done with `File` -> `New document` -> `R Markdown`.

**Exercise:** Create a new R Markdown file. This opens a template. Look closely at its structure. We'll be using them as a guide. 

## YAML options

Look closely at the header of the Markdown template. In any R Markdown document, there's a _header_ written in YAML, which stands for "Yet Another Markup Language" and provides rendering options. 

For instance, you can add the title, the author and the type of output:

```yaml
title: "Working with R Markdown"
author: MYSELF
output: html_document
```

The YAML header can be populated with many options. For instance, to have this notebook's beautiful look, you can give options to the `html_output`, as in the following code chunk. Notice how the options are _indented_. This is important, as indentation is taken into account by YAML. 

```yaml
output: 
  html_document:
    number_sections: true # to 
    highlight: zenburn
    code_folding: show
    df_print: paged
    toc: true
    toc_float:
      collapsed: false
      smooth_scroll: true
```

## Insert a code chunk

- Code can be written in `R chunks`. There's a <kbd>+c</kbd> button that allows you to do that or
with the shortcut <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>Alt</kbd> + <kbd>i</kbd>
- The empty chunk looks like this: 

    ` ```{r}`

    ` ``` ` 

- Here, you can insert some R code. For instance, there's the object `cars`, which contains data on speed and break distance by a car. 

    ` ```{r}`
    
    `cars`
      
    ` ``` ` 
- You can **execute a code chunk** using the _play_ button ▶️ on the right-hand side of the chunk or with the shortcut <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Enter</kbd>.

```{r cars}
cars
```

- This is particularly useful when displaying plots

```{r ploot-cars}
plot(cars)
```

## Play with Chunk options

- Every chunk has some options that you can set with the gear ⚙️ icon at the right-hand side of the chunk or by modifying the arguments of the chunk header.
- For instance, you can avoid displaying the code alongside its results by using the option `echo=FALSE`. 
```{r, echo = FALSE}
plot(cars)
```
